summary.text: The Bishop's rule is to look at the road a fault has travelled. The sins of women, children and the poor are the fault of the strong, he says, and a society that leaves souls in darkness is guilty of what is done there. After a day on the scaffold beside a condemned man he mutters that death belongs to God alone.

Valjean steals the silver, and the Bishop answers with a gift. He tells the gendarmes he gave it, adds the candlesticks, and says he has bought the man's soul for God. This mercy is not leniency. It lays a claim on the man who receives it.
Javert is the law in human form. He was born in a prison, worships authority and despises anyone who has ever broken a rule. He has no malice. He simply has a rule with no exceptions.

The mayor and the inspector fight over Fantine. Javert sees a prostitute who attacked a citizen. The mayor sees a woman driven onto the street, and tells him the highest law is conscience. He wins by quoting the criminal code, though, not by pleading.
Javert comes with a warrant and refuses three days' grace, and Fantine dies of the shock. On every point the law is in the right, and the result is a death.

A chain-gang passes at dawn: collared men are beaten with cudgels while children laugh behind the wagons. Cosette asks whether they are still men. 'Sometimes,' says Valjean, who once rode in such a wagon himself.

Valjean is given the right to shoot Javert. Instead he cuts the man loose, tells him his address, and fires into the air. He gives the Bishop's gift again, this time to the man who stands for the law.
Javert can neither arrest the man who spared him nor let him go. He finds that there is something above duty and that the law can be wrong, and he has nowhere to stand. He goes into the Seine.

In the galleys Valjean holds a trial inside himself. He finds himself guilty, then finds society more guilty, and condemns it to his hatred. Here conscience is a courtroom, and its verdict has hardened him.

Standing by the sleeping Bishop, Valjean is caught between crushing the old man's skull and kissing his hand. He does neither, takes the silver and runs. Hugo shows a soul as a battlefield, fought over at night.

After the Bishop's gift, Valjean puts his foot on a child's forty sous almost without knowing it. Then he is horrified and searches for the boy in vain. He weeps for the first time in nineteen years, woken by his own small, mean act.

In 'A Tempest in a Skull', another man is about to go to the galleys under his name. Every argument for keeping silent is a good one: a town that depends on him, Fantine, Cosette. Hugo calls this the struggle with conscience, and shows it can go round all night without an end.
He stands up in court and names himself. His hair has turned white in an hour, and doing the right thing costs him everything he built.

Valjean reads Marius's farewell and feels a frightful joy: the young man who stands between him and Cosette is going to his death of his own accord, and he need only keep the letter in his pocket. An hour later he puts on his uniform and goes out towards the fighting.

The night after the wedding the old struggle comes back, like Jacob wrestling the angel. He can keep his place beside Cosette with his past hidden, or tell the truth and lose her. The chapter does not say which he chooses.
He tells Marius he is an ex-convict named Jean Valjean. No one suspected him and no one was asking. He owes this confession only to himself.

The story starts with a loaf of bread. A pruner steals it for his sister's seven hungry children and pays with nineteen years in the galleys. Hunger caused the crime, and the law took no notice of the hunger.
Cosette, at five, is the inn's drudge and eats under the table with the dog and cat. To be poor here means to be unprotected, not only hungry.

Fantine sells her hair, then her teeth, then herself, and every step down is taken for her child. Hugo names what has happened: slavery has not left Europe. It weighs on women, and it is called prostitution.
Hundreds of abandoned children are picked up in Paris every year. Hugo's gamin is ragged, witty and somehow still innocent, and he calls him a disease that light and education must cure.

Marius learns poverty from the inside: days without bread, and a coat he wears only after dark so that it passes for black. For a proud young man it is hard but bearable, even ennobling. Hugo calls the book 'The Excellence of Misfortune'.

Through a hole in the wall Marius sees misery that has turned vicious. A father stages his family's poverty for a visitor, and a daughter cuts her hand on a pane he made her break. Hugo has just described the lowest depth, where ignorance and want breed crime, and this garret is that depth in a single room.
Hugo sets out his programme: education, work as a right, limits on poverty without limits on wealth. A society no longer needs to fear a peasants' revolt, he says, but it can die slowly of misery.

In the Luxembourg a well-fed bourgeois throws a brioche to the swans to teach his son a lesson about plenty. Two lost little boys fish it out of the water, and the elder gives his brother the larger half.
Tholomyès is Fantine's first and only love. To him she is the pleasure of one summer. The book's first love story is lopsided from the start.

Marius falls in love with a girl whose name he does not know. It happens through glances along an alley of the Luxembourg, and soon he is worshipping an initial on a handkerchief. Hugo makes it comic and total at once.
The elder Jondrette girl offers to help Marius in anything, though she knows perfectly well it is the other girl he wants. Hers is a love that works for its own defeat.
The notebook under the stone is unsigned, and its love fills the universe: it reduces the whole world to one being. Hugo lets this devotion speak at length, almost as a prayer.

In the Rue Plumet garden the lovers are chaste to the point of absurdity. They do not notice the cholera, they have not told each other their pasts, and they never ask where this is leading. Hugo celebrates it and frets about it in the same pages.

Dying in Marius's arms, Éponine confesses that she led him to the barricade so that they would die together, and asks for a kiss on her brow. Her love both wants to possess him and gives its life for him, in one act.
Valjean reads Cosette's note backwards in a mirror and finds hatred in his heart for the young man. His love for her has a jealous side the book had not shown before.

'One Mother Meets Another Mother.' Fantine leaves Cosette with a woman who looks like a good mother because her own little girls are happy on a swing. That mother loves her daughters, and no one else.

At fifty-five Valjean has never been a father, a lover, a husband or a friend. All that pent-up affection rushes towards Cosette, and she calls him father. Hugo says that the Bishop brought him the dawn of virtue, and Cosette brings the dawn of love.

Marius learns that the father he was raised to despise came secretly to church for ten years just to watch him. He turns to that dead man's cause with all the force of guilt and love, too late to tell him.

Gavroche calls at the Gorbeau house to see 'his ancestors' and hears that his whole family is in prison. He says 'Ah!', spins on his heel and goes off singing. A child his parents never loved has made the street his family.

M. Gillenormand has pined for his grandson for four years. When Marius finally comes, the old man greets him harshly and wrecks the meeting, then collapses calling his name. Pride and love live side by side in him.
'How from a Brother One Becomes a Father.' An abandoned child feeds his little brother. Being a parent is something you do, the chapter suggests, not something blood owes you.

Valjean makes Cosette call him 'Monsieur Jean' and gently detaches her from himself. When she slips and says 'father', he corrects her and turns away to hide his tears. A father is undoing his own fatherhood.
On his deathbed Valjean gives Cosette the one thing he had kept from her: her mother's name, Fantine. The two parents the book began with meet at last in her.

The dying conventionary G— says he voted for the death of the tyrant ignorance, of prostitution, of the night of childhood. The Bishop arrives cold and ends on his knees asking the old man's blessing. The Revolution enters the book as an argument that the saint loses.

Hugo refuses to be glad about Waterloo, which he sees as a victory of the kings over the Revolution. Yet progress cannot be stopped, he says: the restored monarchy is forced to be liberal in spite of itself.
From inside the convent Hugo states his rule. Respect the past if it consents to be dead. Fight it when it insists on living.

Marius, a new convert, defends Napoleon's glory at the Café Musain. Combeferre answers with two words, 'To be free', and Enjolras says, 'My mother is the Republic.' Glory and liberty turn out to be different causes.
Hugo draws a line between insurrection, the whole nation against a usurping part, and revolt, a part against the whole. He leaves open which one June 1832 was.
Old Mabeuf came along only because fighting the government seemed 'good'. He climbs the barricade with the flag and is shot. Enjolras holds up his bullet-torn coat: this is their flag now.

Enjolras imagines the future aloud: a happy twentieth century with schools for all, no scaffold and no war. The barricade is a heap of ideas and a heap of woes, he says, and those who die on it enter a tomb flooded with dawn.

Paris has shut its doors on the insurgents. Hugo weighs a utopia that takes up arms too soon, and admits that every blade has two edges. Then he names the subject of his whole book: the march from evil to good, from night to day, from appetite to conscience.
Hugo builds Paris in 1817 out of its fashions, scandals, songs and gossip. A city is a year as well as a place.
A chase by moonlight runs through streets that Hugo says have since vanished. He maps them from memory and old plans, as though describing a lost city.

'Ecce Paris, ecce homo.' The gamin is the city in small, and the city is all of history in brief: Athens, Rome and Jerusalem at once. It laughs at everything, and Hugo adds grimly that it would miss its guillotine.
Under Paris Hugo imagines society honeycombed with mines, dug by thinkers and reformers. Beneath them all lies a lightless pit of crime.
During a rising most of Paris goes on shopping and going to the theatre, calling it 'a squabble in the Rue Saint-Martin'. This time, though, the great city is afraid.
Seen from an owl's height, the insurgent quarter is a black hole in the lit city, with the bayonets closing in around it.
The rest of Paris does not rise. A leaden indifference settles over the men on the barricade, and the city that makes revolutions leaves them on their own.
Under the city of light lies the city of mud. Hugo calls the sewer the conscience of the city, the one place where nothing is disguised and everything confesses.
At night the Bishop sits in his little garden under the stars. He does not study God; he is dazzled by him. Light, for him, is close to love.
In 'Billows and Shadows' a man falls overboard into the night sea while the ship sails on. Society's penal law, Hugo says, throws souls into the dark like this.
Valjean bends over the sleeping Bishop, whose face is lit by a shaft of moonlight, and for a moment the light holds him back.
Cosette walks alone into the black forest with a bucket bigger than she is, under a red, setting planet. Here darkness is pure terror, until a hand lifts the weight out of hers.
'Lux Facta Est', 'let there be light': the awkward girl of the Luxembourg has become a beautiful young woman. Love arrives in this book as a dawn.
In the lowest depths Hugo puts it plainly: the only social danger is darkness, and the only cure is light, by which he means teaching people. Destroy ignorance and you destroy crime.
In the sewer Valjean sinks into black mud until only his head is above it, holding Marius up the whole time. When his foot finds stone again he climbs out and prays.
'A Night Behind Which There Is Day.' Valjean dies beside the Bishop's candlesticks, which he had lit in broad daylight. The light given in the first book is still burning at the end.
Hugo argues that a night of rain lost Napoleon Waterloo. The wet ground delayed his guns and gave Blücher time to arrive. History turns on accidents.
The hollow road of Ohain, invisible from the French side, swallows the cuirassiers rank after rank. Hugo's verdict is that God had decided Napoleon's fall, and no genius could have stopped it.
The real victor of Waterloo, Hugo says, is not an emperor or a duke. It is an obscure officer who answers catastrophe with a single obscene word. The great men shrink and the unknown man looms.
After the battle a marauder robs a wounded officer, drags him alive from under the dead, and is thanked as a rescuer. The great day ends in a small private lie.
The colonel's note asks his son to do good to a sergeant named Thénardier who 'saved his life'. A false debt from the battlefield passes from father to son.

Marius hears that the man his father told him to honour is about to murder the man he has been watching, and he cannot bring himself to fire. A lie told on the battlefield of Waterloo paralyses a young man in a Paris garret years later.
In 'Facts Whence History Springs and Which History Ignores', Hugo rebuilds the spring of 1832 from police reports and oaths sworn in wine-shops. This is the history that the textbooks leave out.
Defending his chapters on thieves' slang, Hugo claims that the historian of a society's depths has as grave a duty as the historian of its battles and kings.
The traveller announces himself before anyone asks: Jean Valjean, a convict with a yellow passport. His name is his sentence, and he throws it at his hosts like a challenge.
A stranger with no passport remakes a whole town and is known only as Father Madeleine. No one asks where he came from. He is known only by what he has done.
Madeleine is Jean Valjean, and another man is about to become Jean Valjean in his place. Champmathieu is being condemned for a name.
'I am Jean Valjean.' He takes his name back in open court, and with it the galleys.
At the convent he becomes Ultime Fauchelevent, borrowing his name from the old man he once saved from under a cart.
Jondrette, Fabantou and the rest throw off their aliases: 'My name is Thénardier!' For him names are tools, put on and dropped as needed.

Valjean has Cosette call him 'Monsieur Jean', which is neither her father's name nor his own, and he calls her 'Madame'. He is putting on a new mask, and this one seems meant to make her let go of him.
In a far corner of Père-Lachaise lies a stone with no name on it. Even the four lines once pencilled there have been washed away by the rain.
